subtopics.title: Hand moulding tools
subtopics.theory_md: **Shovel** mixes and moves sand. **Riddle** is a wire-mesh sieve that removes lumps. **Rammer**: **peen** (wedge) end packs sand near the pattern and in corners, **butt** (flat) end rams the top. **Strike-off bar** levels sand with the box top. **Sprue pin** and riser pin form the sprue and riser. **Vent wire** pierces vents for gas. **Draw spike** and rapping plate loosen and lift the pattern. **Lifter** cleans deep pockets and the bottom. **Trowel and slick** finish and repair surfaces. **Gate cutter** cuts the runner and ingate. **Swab** wets the edges before the pattern is drawn. **Bellows** blows out loose sand. **Gaggers** support hanging sand in the cope.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of making a sandcastle in a bucket: you sieve the sand, press it in, scrape the top flat, poke air holes and lift the shape out. Each foundry tool does one of these jobs.
key_points: Riddle sieves sand; shovel mixes it; rammer has a peen end (near pattern) and a butt end (top)
Strike-off bar levels the sand; sprue pin and riser pin form the sprue and riser
Vent wire makes vent holes; draw spike and rapping plate loosen and withdraw the pattern
Lifter, trowel and slick finish the cavity; gate cutter cuts runner and ingate
Swab wets the edges; bellows blows out loose sand

subtopics.title: Flasks, furnaces and what the foundry shop does
subtopics.theory_md:
The **foundry shop** makes **castings**: metal is melted, poured into a mould cavity and solidifies in its shape. Complex shapes (engine blocks, machine beds, pipes, pulleys) and one-off or heavy parts are cheap to cast.

**Flask (moulding box)**: wooden or metal frame. The top box is the **cope**, the bottom box the **drag**, a box between them the **cheek** (three-part mould). Pins and lugs align them. The **moulding board** carries the pattern and drag.

**Melting**: **cupola** for cast iron, crucible or pit furnace for non-ferrous metals, electric furnace for steel. **Ladles**, crucibles and tongs carry and pour the metal.
subtopics.basics_md: A flask is like a sandwich: bread on top (cope), bread below (drag), and a filling box (cheek) if you need a thicker sandwich.
key_points: Foundry shop makes castings: melt, pour into a mould, solidify, fettle
Cope = top box, drag = bottom box, cheek = intermediate box
Cupola melts cast iron; crucible or pit furnace melts non-ferrous metals
Moulding board supports the pattern and drag during ramming

**Pins and lugs** align the boxes so that the two halves of the cavity match and the mould does not shift.

subtopics.title: Pattern, core print and colour code
subtopics.theory_md:
A **pattern** is a replica of the object to be cast; it forms the mould cavity. It is **not identical to the casting**: it is larger by the **allowances**, carries **core prints**, may be split or have loose pieces, and cored holes are not shown.

**Core print**: a projection on the pattern that leaves a seat in the mould to locate and support the core.

**Colour code** (common convention): unmachined (as cast) surfaces **black**; surfaces to be machined **red**; core prints **yellow**; loose-piece seats **red stripes on yellow**; stop-offs **black stripes on yellow**.

Casting weight from a solid pattern: $W_c \approx W_p\,\rho_{metal}/\rho_{pattern}$.
subtopics.basics_md: A pattern is the cookie cutter. You press it into sand to leave a hole of the same shape, then fill the hole with metal. The cutter must be slightly bigger because the metal shrinks.
key_points: Pattern = replica of the casting used to make the mould cavity, larger by allowances
Pattern differs from casting: allowances, core prints, split or loose pieces, no cored holes
Core print locates and supports the core
Colour code: black unmachined, red machined, yellow core prints
Casting weight = pattern weight x (density of metal / density of pattern material)

questions.model_answer_md:

2. **Core prints**: the pattern has them; the casting has none.
3. **Holes**: cored holes are not on the pattern; cores make them.
4. **Construction**: pattern may be split or have loose pieces; casting is one piece.
5. **Draft**: pattern faces are tapered for withdrawal.
6. **Material and finish**: wood, metal or plastic painted to the colour code, against cast metal.

questions.q: A brass pattern weighs 0.8 kg. Estimate the weight of the casting of the same shape in aluminium. (Brass 8.5 g/cc, aluminium 2.7 g/cc; ignore allowances.)
questions.model_answer_md:
Same volume, so weight scales with density.

$W_c = W_p\,\dfrac{\rho_{Al}}{\rho_{brass}} = 0.8 \times \dfrac{2.7}{8.5} = 0.254\ \text{kg}$

Check on the reverse: a pine pattern of 1.5 kg (0.5 g/cc) gives a cast iron (7.2 g/cc) casting of $1.5\times 7.2/0.5 = 21.6$ kg.
points: Volume of casting = volume of pattern
$W_c = W_p \rho_{casting}/\rho_{pattern}$
Substitution 0.8 x 2.7/8.5
Answer 0.254 kg with unit

questions.q: A pine pattern weighs 1.5 kg. Estimate the cast iron casting weight, and say why the real casting is lighter. (Pine 0.5 g/cc, cast iron 7.2 g/cc.)
questions.model_answer_md:
$W_c \approx 1.5\times\dfrac{7.2}{0.5} = 1.5 \times 14.4 = 21.6\ \text{kg}$

The real casting is lighter than this because the pattern is oversize by the allowances, and cored holes (not on the pattern) remove metal.
points: Formula $W_c = W_p \rho_{CI}/\rho_{pine}$
Pattern oversize by allowances and cored holes make the casting lighter

subtopics.title: Pattern materials and selection
subtopics.theory_md:
**Wood** (pine, deodar, teak, mahogany): cheap, light, easy to shape and repair; absorbs moisture, warps and wears. For few castings and large patterns.
**Metals** (aluminium, brass, cast iron, steel): accurate, durable, smooth, dimensionally stable; costly and heavier. For mass production and machine moulding.
**Plastics** (epoxy, polyurethane): light, smooth, moisture-proof.
**Plaster of Paris**: intricate small patterns, brittle.
**Wax**: investment casting; **polystyrene**: lost foam; both are melted or vaporised, not withdrawn.

**Selection criteria**: number of castings, size and complexity, accuracy and finish, strength and wear, dimensional stability, weight, ease of working and repair, cost, moulding method.
subtopics.basics_md: If you need one birthday cake, a cardboard cutter is fine. If you need a million biscuits, you buy a steel cutter. Pattern material follows the number of castings you need.
key_points: Wood: cheap, easy, warps and wears; for small runs and large patterns
Metal (Al, brass, CI, steel): durable, accurate; for mass production and machine moulding
Plastic, plaster of Paris, wax (investment), polystyrene (lost foam)
Selection: quantity, size and complexity, accuracy, finish, cost, workability, repair, moulding method

- Merits: cheap, light, easy to shape and repair, suits small runs and large patterns.
- Demerits: absorbs moisture, warps, wears quickly, short life.

**Metal** (aluminium, brass, cast iron, steel)
- Merits: accurate, durable, smooth, no moisture problem, suits machine moulding.
- Demerits: costly, heavy (except aluminium), hard to repair or alter.

**Selection factors**: number of castings, size and complexity, accuracy and finish, cost, ease of working and repair, wear resistance, moulding method.

subtopics.title: Making a pattern: soap case and crankshaft
subtopics.theory_md:
**Sequence for any pattern**: (1) study the drawing; (2) choose the **parting line** and the pattern type; (3) choose the material (wood for few castings, aluminium or metal for production); (4) add **allowances** (shrinkage, machining, draft, and so on); (5) mark out, saw, plane and shape; (6) provide **core prints** and a **core box** if the casting is hollow; (7) join halves with **dowel pins**; (8) fillet corners, sand smooth, apply **shellac** and paint to the colour code.

**Soap case**: an open, hollow box; a solid pattern of the outer shape with the parting plane through the open face and the hollow made by a core.
**Crankshaft**: long and with webs, so a **split pattern** with the parting along the axis.
subtopics.basics_md: Making a pattern is just carpentry with a plan: decide where it will be split, make it slightly larger, mark the places that will be machined, and paint it so the moulder reads it at a glance.

Add allowances: shrinkage, machining, draft; round corners with fillets

subtopics.title: Solid, split, loose-piece and match-plate patterns
subtopics.theory_md:
**Solid (single-piece)**: one piece, no joint; simple shapes with one flat face, few castings (spanner, block, bracket, handwheel).
**Split (two-piece)**: cut along the parting line into two halves joined by **dowel pins**; one half in the drag, one in the cope. For complex shapes with cavities on both sides: pipe fittings, cylinders, valve bodies, pulleys.
**Loose-piece**: a projection or boss is fixed with a **wooden pin** and drawn sideways after the main body.
**Match-plate**: cope and drag halves mounted on the two sides of a metal plate, often with gating; **mass production of small castings** on machines.
**Cope-and-drag**: halves on separate plates, for large castings.
subtopics.basics_md: Moulding must let the pattern slide out of the sand. Simple shapes slide out whole. Awkward shapes are cut in two or have detachable bits so each part can leave on its own.
key_points: Solid: one piece, simple shape, small numbers (spanner, block)
Split: two halves joined by dowel pins, cope and drag halves; pipes, cylinders, valve bodies
Loose-piece: projections held by pins and drawn out after the main body
Match-plate: both halves on one plate for mass production of small castings
Cope-and-drag: separate plates for large castings

subtopics.title: Sweep, skeleton, segmental and other patterns
subtopics.theory_md:
**Sweep**: a board cut to the profile, rotated about a spindle to sweep out the mould cavity; large **axisymmetric** castings (bells, kettles, large pulleys).
**Skeleton**: a wooden framework of ribs, filled with sand or loam and strickled; large castings in small numbers (water pipes, bends, turbine casings).
**Segmental**: a segment of the shape rotated about a centre and indexed to form a circular mould (large gears, rings).
**Gated**: several patterns joined by gates and runners, many small castings in one mould.
**Follow-board**: a board shaped to support a thin or weak pattern during ramming.

The common point of sweep, skeleton and segmental patterns: they save the cost of a full solid pattern for big jobs.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine spinning a template round a post to scrape out a round hole in sand. That is a sweep. A skeleton is the same idea but built as a ribbed frame, like the bones of the shape.
key_points: Sweep: profile board rotated on a spindle, for large symmetric castings like bells
Skeleton: ribbed frame filled with sand or loam, large castings in small numbers

Gated: several patterns with gates, multiple small castings per mould

subtopics.title: Shrinkage allowance, shrink rule and the three shrinkages
subtopics.theory_md:
Metal contracts in three stages: **liquid shrinkage** (pouring to freezing temperature), **solidification shrinkage** (liquid to solid) and **solid shrinkage** (freezing temperature to room temperature).

The **riser** (and chills) feed the first two. The **shrinkage allowance** on the pattern covers only **solid shrinkage**: the pattern is made larger, $L_p = L_c(1+s)$.

Typical values: grey cast iron about **10 mm/m**, steel about **20 mm/m**, aluminium about 13 mm/m, brass about 15 mm/m.

A **shrink rule** has graduations longer than standard by the shrinkage, so the pattern maker reads the casting size directly.
subtopics.basics_md: A cooling metal bar gets shorter, like a balloon losing air. To end with a 1 m casting you must start with a mould slightly longer than 1 m, so the pattern is made a little bigger.
key_points: Three shrinkages: liquid, solidification, solid
Risers feed liquid and solidification shrinkage; allowance covers solid shrinkage only
Pattern larger by s: CI about 10 mm/m, steel about 20 mm/m
Shrink rule is longer than a standard rule by the shrinkage

2. **Solidification shrinkage**: contraction as liquid turns solid; fed by the **riser** (with chills for directional solidification).
3. **Solid shrinkage**: contraction from freezing temperature to room temperature; allowed for by the **shrinkage allowance** on the pattern (shrink rule).

subtopics.title: Machining and draft allowance, with a worked pattern size
subtopics.theory_md:
**Machining (finish) allowance**: extra metal on surfaces to be machined, because cast surfaces are rough and scaled. Roughly 2 to 6 mm for cast iron, more for steel, 1.5 to 3 mm for non-ferrous. It is **added** to external faces and **subtracted** from holes.

**Draft (taper) allowance**: a taper of **1 to 3 degrees** on faces parallel to the withdrawal direction, so the pattern lifts without breaking the sand. Internal faces need more. Offset $x = h\tan\theta$.

Order of working: finished size, add machining (subtract for holes), then apply $(1+s)$.
subtopics.basics_md: A cast surface comes out rough, like a baked loaf crust. Machining shaves it off, so you start with extra thickness. Draft is the slope that lets a cup slide out of its mould.
key_points: Machining allowance: added on external faces, subtracted for holes
Draft: 1 to 3 degrees on faces along the withdrawal direction, more on internal faces
Draft offset $x = h\tan\theta$
Pattern size = (finished size + machining) x (1 + s)

subtopics.title: Distortion, shake and the full list of allowances
subtopics.theory_md:
**Distortion (camber) allowance**: long flat plates and U or V shapes warp on cooling because thin and thick parts contract unevenly. The pattern is bent in the **opposite direction** by the expected amount.

**Shake (rapping) allowance**: the pattern is rapped to loosen it, which **enlarges** the cavity, so the pattern is made slightly **smaller**. It is the only **negative** allowance.

**All five allowances**: shrinkage, machining, draft, distortion, shake. Shrinkage, machining and draft are positive (pattern bigger); distortion is a reverse bend; shake is negative.
subtopics.basics_md: Rapping a stuck pattern to free it widens the hole a bit, like wiggling a cork out of a bottle. So you make the pattern a little small to cancel that.
key_points: Five allowances: shrinkage, machining, draft, distortion, shake
Distortion: pattern bent opposite to the expected warp (U, V shapes, long plates)
Shake: rapping enlarges the cavity, so the allowance is negative

subtopics.title: Green sand composition and types of sand
subtopics.theory_md:
**Green moulding sand**: silica sand (SiO$_2$) 75 to 85% (refractory grains); clay 10 to 15% (bentonite or fireclay, binder); water 2 to 8% (activates the clay, commonly 4 to 6%); additives a few % (sea coal for finish, cereal or dextrin for strength, wood flour for collapsibility).

**Types of sand by use**: **facing sand** (fresh, fine, next to the pattern), **backing or floor sand** (used sand that fills the box), **system sand** (machine moulding), **parting sand** (dry, clay-free silica, stops cope and drag sticking), **loam sand** (about 50% clay, large castings), **core sand** (sand with oil or resin binder).
subtopics.basics_md: Sand alone does not stick. Add clay and water and it behaves like wet beach sand that holds a shape. That is green sand: 'green' means moist, not green coloured.
key_points: Silica 75 to 85%, clay 10 to 15%, water 2 to 8%, additives a few %
Silica gives refractoriness, clay is the binder, water activates clay
Facing, backing, system, parting, loam and core sand
Parting sand is dry silica with no clay; green means moist

subtopics.title: Properties of moulding sand and additives
subtopics.theory_md:
**Refractoriness**: does not fuse at pouring temperature. **Permeability**: lets steam and gas escape (low gives blowholes). **Cohesiveness**: grains stick to each other. **Adhesiveness**: sand sticks to the flask walls. **Strength**: green, dry and hot strength. **Flowability (plasticity)**: packs round the pattern. **Collapsibility**: gives way to the shrinking casting (low gives hot tears). Also fineness for finish, reusability, low cost.

**Additives**: **sea coal** (coal dust) for surface finish and to stop metal sticking; **cereal or dextrin** for dry strength; **wood flour or sawdust** for collapsibility and permeability; **molasses, pitch** for strength; **bentonite, fireclay** as binders; **silica flour** for hot strength.
subtopics.basics_md: Every property answers one problem: gas must escape, the mould must hold its shape, survive heat, and then crumble away so the cooling casting is not squeezed.
key_points: Refractoriness, permeability, cohesiveness, adhesiveness, strength, flowability, collapsibility
Low permeability gives blowholes; low collapsibility gives hot tears
Silica is common: refractory, cheap, plentiful, reusable
Sea coal gives finish, cereal gives strength, wood flour gives collapsibility

subtopics.title: Permeability number calculation
subtopics.theory_md:
**Permeability number** $P = \dfrac{V\,H}{p\,A\,t}$ with $V$ volume of air (cc), $H$ height of specimen (cm), $p$ air pressure (g/cm$^2$), $A$ cross-section area (cm$^2$), $t$ time (min).

Standard specimen: 50.8 mm diameter x 50.8 mm high ($H = 5.08$ cm, $A = 20.268$ cm$^2$), air volume $V = 2000$ cc. Then $P = \dfrac{501.28}{p\,t}$.

A higher $P$ means gas escapes more easily. Too high gives rough surface and metal penetration; too low gives blowholes.
subtopics.basics_md: Blow air through a sand plug and time it. The faster the air gets through, the more open the sand is, and the higher its permeability number.
key_points: $P = VH/(pAt)$ with t in minutes and p in g/cm$^2$
Standard specimen 50.8 mm x 50.8 mm, 2000 cc air: $P = 501.28/(pt)$
High P gives rough finish, low P gives blowholes

questions.why: The constant 501.28 uses time in minutes and pressure in g/cm$^2$.

questions.q: In a permeability test on a standard specimen (50.8 mm dia x 50.8 mm high), 2000 cc of air passed in 1.2 min at 5 g/cm$^2$. Find the permeability number.
points: Correct formula

questions.q: A standard specimen passes 2000 cc of air in 1.5 min at a pressure of 8 g/cm$^2$. Find P, and say how it compares with the 83.5 sand above.
questions.model_answer_md:
$P = \dfrac{501.28}{p\,t} = \dfrac{501.28}{8\times 1.5} = \dfrac{501.28}{12} = 41.8$

It is about half of 83.5, so this sand is less permeable (more blowhole risk).
points: P about 41.8
Lower permeability than 83.5

subtopics.title: Expendable and permanent moulds
subtopics.theory_md:
**Expendable moulds** are destroyed to remove the casting: sand (green, dry, skin-dried, loam, core sand), **CO$_2$**, **shell**, **investment (lost wax)**, plaster and cement-bonded moulds.

**Permanent moulds** are metal (cast iron or steel) dies reused for thousands of castings: gravity die casting, pressure die casting, centrifugal casting; mostly for non-ferrous metals.

By position in the shop: **bench**, **floor**, **pit** and **machine** moulds (details under Moulding processes).

Expendable moulds allow complex shapes and any metal; permanent moulds give a better finish and faster production but cost more for tooling.
subtopics.basics_md: A sand mould is broken every time you want the casting out, like cracking an egg. A metal die opens like a waffle iron and is used again and again.
key_points: Expendable: sand, CO2, shell, investment, plaster; destroyed after one casting
Permanent: metal dies reused many times (die, centrifugal casting)
By position: bench, floor, pit, machine
Metal moulds are not expendable

subtopics.title: Making a two-box green sand mould
subtopics.theory_md:
**Drag**: pattern half flat on the **moulding board**, drag box upside down round it; sprinkle **parting sand**; riddle 20 to 30 mm of **facing sand**; fill **backing sand** and **ram** (peen end near the pattern, butt end on top); **strike off**; **vent**; **roll over**.

**Cope**: set the cope pattern half on the dowels; parting sand; cope box; **sprue pin** and **riser pin**; riddle, fill, ram, strike off, vent; pull the pins; cut the pouring basin.

**Finish**: lift cope, **swab** edges, **rap and draw** the pattern, cut **runner and ingate**, repair, set the **core**, close the mould, clamp or weight the cope, **pour**.

Too soft ramming gives swells; too hard gives blowholes.
subtopics.basics_md: Press the pattern into sand in two halves, like making a hollow chocolate from two moulds, then lift the pattern out, join the halves and pour.

questions.q: Why are weights placed on the cope before pouring? Find the lifting force for a parting area of 0.04 m$^2$ with 0.15 m of cast iron (7000 kg/m$^3$) above it.
questions.model_answer_md:
Molten metal presses up on the cope over the parting area; if the force exceeds the cope's weight, the cope lifts and metal runs out at the parting line.

$F = \rho g h A = 7000\times 9.81\times 0.15\times 0.04 = 412\ \text{N}$ (about 42 kgf)

The cope plus weights must exceed this, with a margin.

subtopics.title: The casting process, mould parts and fettling
subtopics.theory_md:
**Casting**: pour molten metal into a cavity, let it solidify, remove and clean it.
**Sequence**: pattern making, moulding (with cores), melting, pouring, solidification, shake-out, fettling, inspection.

**Elements of a sand mould**: cope, drag, (cheek), parting line, pouring basin, sprue, runner, gate (ingate), riser, cavity, core and core prints, vents, chaplets, chills.

**Post-casting**: knock out; cut off gates and risers; clean by shot or sand blasting; fettle (grind fins); inspect (visual, dye penetrant, X-ray); heat treat; repair; machine.

**Classification of manufacturing processes**: casting; forming (forging, rolling, extrusion, drawing); machining; joining (welding, brazing, riveting); finishing; powder metallurgy and plastic moulding.
subtopics.basics_md: Casting is like making an ice cube: shape a hole, fill it with liquid, wait, pop it out and trim the rough edges.

subtopics.title: Gating: tapered sprue, runner, ingate
subtopics.theory_md:
**Gating system**: pouring basin, **sprue**, sprue well, **runner**, **ingates**, cavity.
- **Sprue**: the vertical channel from the basin down to the runner.
- **Runner**: the horizontal channel in the parting plane that carries metal from the sprue base to the ingates and round the cavity.

**Why the sprue is tapered**: falling metal speeds up, $v=\sqrt{2gh}$, and by continuity $A_1v_1=A_2v_2$ so the area must shrink: $A_1/A_2=\sqrt{h_2/h_1}$. A straight sprue cannot run full; the stream pulls away from the wall and sucks air in (**aspiration**), causing **air entrapment, gas porosity, oxide inclusions and sand erosion**. The taper keeps it full.
subtopics.basics_md: Water from a tap thins as it falls. A sprue that narrows downwards matches the thinning stream, so it stays full and does not drag air in with it.
key_points: Sprue vertical, runner horizontal; metal goes basin, sprue, well, runner, ingate, cavity
Taper from continuity: area falls as velocity $\sqrt{2gh}$ rises
Cylindrical sprue causes aspiration: air entrapment, porosity, oxide inclusions, erosion
Gating must fill quietly and trap slag

subtopics.title: Riser: purpose, size, shape and location
subtopics.theory_md:
A **riser** (feeder head) is a reservoir of molten metal that feeds the casting as it shrinks, so the shrinkage cavity forms in the riser, not the casting. It also lets gas and slag escape and shows the mould is full.

**Size**: Chvorinov's rule, $t = B\,(V/A)^2$. The riser must freeze **after** the casting, so $(V/A)_{riser}\ge 1.2\,(V/A)_{casting}$ and it must hold enough metal for the shrinkage.
**Shape**: cylindrical, $H/D$ about 1 to 1.5, best $V/A$; open or blind.
**Location**: on or beside the **heaviest section** (last to freeze), usually the cope, with directional solidification towards the riser; short thick neck.
subtopics.basics_md: The riser is a spare tank of hot metal sitting on the thickest part. As the casting shrinks it drinks from the tank, and the tank must stay liquid longer than the casting.
key_points: Riser feeds shrinkage so the cavity forms in the riser
Chvorinov: $t=B(V/A)^2$; riser must freeze later than the casting
Riser $V/A$ at least 1.2 x casting $V/A$
Cylindrical, H/D about 1 to 1.5; open or blind
Placed on the heaviest section; top (cope) so gravity helps

questions.q: A cubic casting of side 100 mm is fed by a cylindrical riser with H = D that cools from all surfaces. Find the casting V/A, and the minimum riser diameter using a factor 1.2. Also find the ratio of riser to casting solidification times.
questions.model_answer_md:
Cube: $V/A = a^3/6a^2 = a/6 = 100/6 = 16.67$ mm.

Riser must have $V/A \ge 1.2\times16.67 = 20$ mm.

Cylinder with $H=D$ and all surfaces cooling: $V=\pi D^3/4$, $A=\pi D^2/2+\pi D^2=1.5\pi D^2$, so $V/A = D/6$.

$D/6 = 20$ gives **$D = 120$ mm** (H = 120 mm).

Time ratio $= (1.2)^2 = 1.44$, so the riser freezes 44% later than the casting.

Required riser V/A = 20 mm

subtopics.title: Bench, floor, pit and machine moulding
subtopics.theory_md:
**By where and how the mould is made**
- **Bench moulding**: small flasks on a bench; small castings.
- **Floor moulding**: medium to large moulds on the foundry floor; the floor may serve as the drag.
- **Pit moulding**: very large castings in a pit; the pit is the drag, with a cope on top.
- **Machine moulding**: mass production. **Jolt**: sand densest near the pattern. **Squeeze**: densest at the top. **Jolt-squeeze**: uniform. **Sand slinger**: throws sand at high speed for large moulds.

By sand or mould type the moulds are green, dry, skin-dried, loam and core sand; special processes follow in the next subtopic.

subtopics.title: CO2, shell, investment and lost-foam moulding
subtopics.theory_md:
**CO$_2$ moulding**: sand with 3 to 6% **sodium silicate**, hardened in seconds by CO$_2$ gas: $\mathrm{Na_2SiO_3 + CO_2 \rightarrow Na_2CO_3 + SiO_2}$ (gel). Quick and strong; poor collapsibility.

**Shell moulding (Croning)**: sand with 3 to 8% **phenolic resin** falls on a metal pattern heated to about 200 to 250 C and forms a 5 to 10 mm shell; two shells are clamped. Good finish and accuracy, mass production.

**Investment (lost wax)**: wax pattern, ceramic coating, wax melted out, shell fired, metal poured; intricate precise parts (turbine blades, jewellery).

**Lost foam**: polystyrene pattern vaporised by the metal.
subtopics.basics_md: In each special process the sand is made stiffer or finer than usual: set by gas, baked as a thin resin shell, or replaced by a ceramic coating over a wax model.
key_points: CO2: sodium silicate sand hardened by CO2 gas
Shell: resin-coated sand on a heated metal pattern forms a thin shell
Investment: wax pattern melted out of ceramic shell; intricate parts

questions.q: Write short notes on shell moulding and CO$_2$ moulding.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Shell moulding**
1. Metal pattern heated to about 200 to 250 C.
2. Sand with 3 to 8% phenolic resin is dropped on it; a 5 to 10 mm shell cures.
3. The shell is stripped, two halves are clamped and poured.
Advantages: good finish and accuracy, mass production. Limits: costly pattern and resin.

**CO$_2$ moulding**
1. Sand mixed with 3 to 6% sodium silicate is rammed round the pattern.
2. CO$_2$ is passed through it; $\mathrm{Na_2SiO_3 + CO_2 \rightarrow Na_2CO_3 + SiO_2}$ gel hardens it in seconds.
Advantages: fast, strong, accurate. Limit: poor collapsibility.

subtopics.title: Casting defects: cause and remedy
subtopics.theory_md:
| Defect | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| **Blowholes** (smooth gas cavities) | Moisture, low permeability, hard ramming, poor venting | Control moisture, vent, ram evenly |
| **Shrinkage cavity** (rough, at heavy section) | Poor feeding | Proper riser, chills |
| **Misrun** (cavity not filled) | Cold metal, slow pouring | Hotter, faster pour, better gating |
| **Cold shut** (two streams do not fuse) | Same | Same |
| **Hot tear** | Restrained contraction | Collapsible sand, fillets |
| **Mould or core shift** | Misaligned flasks or cores | Good pins, core prints, chaplets |
| **Swell** | Soft ramming | Ram uniformly |
| **Scab, rat tail, buckle** | Sand expansion on the face | Wood flour, softer ramming |
subtopics.basics_md: Every defect has a story: gas that cannot leave, metal that cannot reach, metal that cannot shrink freely, or a mould that moved. Name the story and the cure follows.
key_points: Blowholes: gas, from moisture, low permeability, hard ramming
Shrinkage cavity: poor feeding, cure by riser and chills
Misrun and cold shut: low temperature or slow pouring
Hot tear: restrained contraction; shift: misalignment; swell: soft ramming

questions.q: Explain any five casting defects with causes and remedies.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. **Blowholes**: gas pockets from moisture, low permeability or hard ramming. Remedy: control moisture, vent well, ram evenly.
2. **Shrinkage cavity**: poor feeding at the heaviest section. Remedy: properly sized riser and chills.
3. **Misrun**: metal solidifies before filling the cavity. Remedy: higher pouring temperature, faster pouring, better gating.
4. **Hot tear**: restrained contraction cracks the casting. Remedy: collapsible sand, fillets, uniform sections.
5. **Mould shift**: cope and drag misaligned. Remedy: good pins and clamping.
6. **Swell**: soft ramming bulges the mould. Remedy: uniform ramming.
